content:
Earlier this year, I replaced my home's gasoline lawn mower with a robotic mower that can be controlled via iPhone. All you need to do is manually drive the robot around the garden once with your iPhone, and the system will build a virtual map. Once set up, it will automatically mow according to a preset schedule.

Recently, I tried another system called the TerraMow V1000. It uses a completely different navigation method, and after several weeks of testing, I think this system may be more convenient and easier to use for many people.

Automatic Lens Mapping

The biggest difference between the TerraMow V1000 and the Anthbot M9 I previously reviewed lies in how the two understand your garden.

The Anthbot M9 uses RTK base station positioning. During setup, I needed to manually drive the mower along the boundaries with my phone to create the initial map.

The TerraMow V1000, on the other hand, uses a system the manufacturer calls TerraVision 2.0. It has three built-in lenses that can automatically map out the lawn area, without needing to bury boundary wires underground or installing an additional RTK antenna.

The automatic initial mapping process clearly takes longer. But I think this approach may be simpler for people who are not very tech-savvy.

To test this idea, my mother, who lives in another state, set up and used the TerraMow V1000 on her own without asking me for any help. She replied that everything worked fine. Honestly, I was quite skeptical at the time about whether she would have the patience to manually drive the robot along the boundaries and manually mark no-go zones.

The automatic mapping caused a small issue in my front yard. Since there is no fence or other physical barrier between my lawn and my neighbor's lawn, TerraMow initially included part of my neighbor's lawn in the coverage area of my map.

I solved the problem by marking that area as a no-go zone in the app. However, if there is no clearly visible boundary between two lawns, extra care is needed during the initial mapping phase.

Seeing the World Through the Mower's Lens

The lens on TerraMow also supports a feature I've always loved. The iPhone app can show in real time what the mower sees while it's working.

During testing, I used iPhone Mirroring on my Mac to cast the view to a larger window. I could sit comfortably indoors and watch the mower cross the backyard from its own perspective.

This feature is not necessary for automatic mowing, but it makes the robot more interesting and sometimes explains why it slows down or avoids certain objects. The Anthbot M9 does not have a similar lens streaming feature.

The two iPhone apps are quite similar in other respects. Both let you set working schedules, adjust mowing modes, divide zones, mark no-go zones, and remotely control the mower.

Speaking of remote control, TerraMow's design is particularly impressive. In addition to traditional left and right virtual joysticks, its app also offers a single-hand joystick mode. You can hold the iPhone in a normal posture and use your thumb to steer the mower.

Using the phone to manually operate the mower is not the main purpose of either system. Ideally, the robot should run entirely on schedule without human intervention. But TerraMow's joystick is very handy for touching up missed spots.

Sometimes it almost feels like telekinetically controlling the robot (and is quite satisfying). I can let the iPhone hang at my side and, with just a slight thumb movement, send the machine anywhere I want.

All robotic mower apps should copy this control method.

More Aggressive Mowing Performance

To me, the TerraMow V1000 feels more aggressive than the Anthbot M9. During testing, it mowed lower and was noticeably louder while running.

I wouldn't say TerraMow is loud, but the difference between the two is quite obvious. The Anthbot is extremely quiet when operating—even mowing at night with its headlights on, it's easy to forget it's still running.

Since TerraMow relies on lens-based navigation and needs daylight to operate reliably, scheduling daytime mowing becomes even more important.

Out of the box, the V1000 feels solid and hefty, and is also larger than the Anthbot M9. TerraMow includes a garage with the product to cover the charging dock, whereas the Anthbot's garage has to be purchased separately.

Most importantly, TerraMow operates reliably and performs consistently. I relied on it for weeks on end and never had to do any routine mowing myself.

When Smart Mapping Becomes Too Smart

The same kind of visual intelligence that makes TerraMow easy to set up can sometimes backfire.

The mower continuously adjusts its map based on what it sees. Saving these changes after each mow takes some time, during which you cannot perform other operations in the app.

After several days of heavy rain, I ran into an interesting special situation. Part of the garden had standing water, and TerraMow cleverly avoided that area on its next run.

Inside the skipped circular area, weeds grew taller and taller. As time went on, the mower seemed to treat these taller patches as targets to keep avoiding—even after the water had long receded, that patch of lawn was never mowed again.

I used the remote control function in the app to manually drive the mower through the overgrown patch, and the problem was resolved immediately. Once the area returned to a normal lawn appearance, automatic mowing resumed as usual.

Trimming the edges regularly also helps TerraMow handle boundaries more decisively. If tall grass grows in spots with blurry dividing lines, it may be mistaken for an obstacle and excluded from the mowing area.

Anthbot's approach feels less flexible and relies more on user-defined boundaries and obstacles. This method requires more upfront work, but at the same time avoids the situation where the map 'changes its mind' about a certain patch of lawn.

9to5Mac Review

After trying both systems, I lean toward recommending TerraMow's lens-based approach to most people.

For me, underground boundary wires were never a consideration to begin with, and installing an RTK base station means placing, powering, and maintaining extra hardware. TerraMow needs neither.

Its visual navigation is not perfect. Initial mapping takes longer, hard-to-recognize boundaries need manual correction, and its adaptive behavior once mistakenly treated tall grass as a permanent obstacle.

All of these issues can be resolved. In return, the TerraMow V1000 offers easier setup, reliable and consistent automatic mowing, fun real-time lens footage, and the best manual control experience I've seen in any robotic mower app.

I actually quite enjoy gardening, but mowing is the most repetitive part. Handing this task over to a robot gives me more time to handle landscaping, pruning, and detail work, while keeping the lawn neat and beautiful.

The TerraMow V1000 performs excellently in this regard, enough for me to recommend it—especially for those who want a robotic mower but don't want to dig trenches and bury wires, set up an RTK antenna, or walk around the entire garden boundary holding a phone.

The TerraMow V1000 is currently available on Amazon and its official website, priced at $999, with a $200 discount offer. You can also purchase it through TerraMow's official website.
